planting.note: Plant dormant canes or containerized transplants in late winter through early spring; space 3-4 feet apart in rows 8-10 feet apart on a two-wire trellis. Fruiting occurs in the second year from planting, typically ripening early in the blackberry season.

directions: Plant dormant canes 1-2 inches deep in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic soil (pH 6.0-6.5) and train onto a two-wire trellis. Tupy is a vigorous, thorny, erect blackberry developed by the Brazilian agricultural research agency EMBRAPA from Arkansas breeding lines, and it has become one of the most widely planted commercial blackberries in warm-climate regions of Latin America because of its exceptional heat tolerance and productivity under conditions too warm for many U.S.-bred varieties. Berries are large, glossy black, firm, and tart-sweet, ripening early in the season with a long harvest window and heavy yields. Because canes are thorny, plan for careful pruning and picking; remove fruited floricanes after harvest and tie in 4-6 vigorous new primocanes per plant for the following year. Tupy tolerates the intense heat and humidity of the Gulf Coast better than many thornless northern-bred varieties, making it a strong choice for zone 9-10 growers.

common_name: Womack Blackberry (Texas A&M Heat-Tolerant Thorny Blackberry)

planting.note: Plant dormant canes or containerized transplants in late winter through early spring; space 3-4 feet apart in rows 8-10 feet apart on a trellis. Fruiting occurs in the second year from planting, ripening in the main-season window in zones 8-9.

directions: Plant dormant canes 1-2 inches deep in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic soil (pH 6.0-6.5) and train onto a two-wire trellis. Womack is an erect, thorny blackberry released from the Texas A&M blackberry breeding program and bred specifically to withstand the heat, humidity, and disease pressure of Texas and the western Gulf South. It produces medium to large, firm, sweet-tart berries with good flavor and holds up well to summer heat that causes softer varieties to decline in quality. As an older Texas A&M release, it is a dependable, disease-tolerant option where more modern thornless varieties struggle with heat stress. Prune out fruited floricanes after harvest and select vigorous new primocanes to tie in for next year's crop; wear heavy gloves when working the thorny canes.

common_name: Illini Hardy Blackberry (Extreme Cold-Hardy Erect Blackberry)

planting.note: Plant dormant canes or containerized transplants in early to mid-spring after the coldest weather has passed; space 3-4 feet apart in rows 8-10 feet apart. Fruiting occurs in the second year from planting, ripening mid-to-late season.

directions: Plant dormant canes 1-2 inches deep in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic soil (pH 6.0-6.5). Illini Hardy is an erect, thorny blackberry developed at the University of Illinois specifically for reliable cane survival in cold northern winters where most blackberry varieties suffer significant winterkill, tolerating temperatures well below zero without winter cane protection. Berries are medium-sized, firm, and tart-sweet, ripening mid-to-late season with good yields once established. Because the canes are self-supporting and very cold-tolerant, Illini Hardy is a dependable choice for northern growers who want blackberries without the trellising and winter mulching that tender varieties require. Prune out fruited floricanes after harvest and thin new primocanes to the sturdiest 6-8 per plant to keep the planting productive and manageable.
